observations.evidence: Tested `applyRuntimeIncidentEvent` by creating a `retryFallbackApplied` incident with `fallbackRole: "secondary"`. Then fired a `modelChange` event with `modelRole: "primary"` and `resolvedModelIsFallback: false`. `resolveFallbacks` checks `role === null ? incident.role === null : incident.role === role || incident.role === null`. Because the passed role is `"primary"` but the incident role is `"secondary"`, the active incident is skipped and remains active.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that batch imports in Codex and OMP modals intentionally stay open after failures and renaming a session while search filters are active preserves focus correctly.

observations.scenario: Reviewing import failure modal behavior in App.tsx (importCodexSelected and importPendingOmp) on the pinned base.
observations.evidence: Source inspection of src/App.tsx shows modals selectively close via `setCodexOpen(false)` and `setPendingOmpImportPath(null)` only in `else` blocks explicitly when `failures.length === 0` or `!failure`. If failures occur, the logic intentionally leaves the modal open with the selection intact.
observations.result: Establishes that the observed 'stay open on failure' behavior is an explicit design choice in the current codebase, allowing users to manually deselect items rather than forcing them to re-select.

observations.scenario: Reviewing whether renaming a session while search filters are active correctly preserves focus inside the list when navigating via keyboard.
observations.evidence: Executed a local isolated jsdom test simulating the focus interaction when the virtualizer re-renders a list where search filters are applied. The test confirmed that after an internal render cycle, the `actionFocusRef` properly guards focus and `document.activeElement` stays on the rename input.
observations.result: Establishes that focus is properly preserved during virtualized session rename interactions even when a search query actively filters the list. No regression was observed.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items, despite the lack of user workload evidence so far.
Investigate the memory consumption limit of large OMP import sessions when the file contains heavily fragmented chunks.

previous_reports.summary: Identified an accessibility violation in SessionRow where an interactive input is nested inside a role='button' element during renaming.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on a SessionRow component while it is in the 'renaming' state.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a simplified DOM representing the renaming state and via a jsdom test on the SessionRow component itself. Both reported a 'nested-interactive' serious violation because the <input> element is a focusable descendant of <div className='session-select' role='button' tabIndex={0}>. Axe-core also flagged aria-pressed and aria-label on the parent wrapper that don't apply well when presentation role is needed.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI creates an invalid nested interactive element structure during session rename. Removing role='button', tabIndex={0}, and aria-pressed from the parent when renaming=true resolves the violation.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if CodexImportModal and ImportSessionModal landmarks (header/footer) create duplicate banner/contentinfo landmarks when mounted due to role='dialog' overriding their scoping parent's semantic.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that fixing the seriously invalid nested interactive structure in SessionRow and duplicate banner/contentinfo landmarks in CodexImportModal/ImportSessionModal resolves the reported axe-core accessibility violations.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on a SessionRow component while it is in the 'renaming' state with and without the nested-interactive fix.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a jsdom test rendering SessionRow. By default, it reported a 'nested-interactive' serious violation because the <input> element is a focusable descendant of <div className='session-select' role='button' tabIndex={0}>, and a 'label' critical violation. Changing the parent to `role='presentation'` and removing its `tabIndex` when `renaming=true` resolved the nested-interactive violation. Adding `aria-label=t(lang, 'editFixedTitle')` to the input resolved the label violation.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI creates an invalid nested interactive element structure during session rename. Converting role='button' to role='presentation' and dropping tabIndex=0 on the parent when renaming=true resolves the violation and properly exposes the input.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on the app's modals to observe duplicate banner and contentinfo landmarks.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a mocked DOM containing CodexImportModal and ImportSessionModal side-by-side or within a surrounding layout. It flagged 'landmark-no-duplicate-banner', 'landmark-no-duplicate-contentinfo', and 'landmark-unique' moderate violations because the modals use raw <header> and <footer> tags inside their <section role='dialog'> wrappers, which aren't fully sequestered from the global document context when mounted.
observations.result: Establishes that using <header> and <footer> directly inside role='dialog' modals causes duplicate semantic landmarks if multiple are mounted or they conflict with the main application shell. Changing these to <div className='settings-header'> and <div className='settings-actions'> preserves visual layout without polluting global accessibility landmarks.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items, despite the lack of user workload evidence so far.
Investigate the memory consumption limit of large OMP import sessions when the file contains heavily fragmented chunks.

research_result.summary: Verified that a crash during session import leaves state inconsistent across restarts, requiring a recovery protocol.

observations.scenario: Simulating a hard process crash during `commit_import_with` after swapping artifact directories but before the JSONL write completes.
observations.evidence: A custom Rust script testing the atomic boundaries of `commit_import_with` revealed that crashing right before `write_session` leaves the original (old) `session.jsonl` intact while the `session/` directory holds the newly imported artifacts. The old artifacts are isolated in `session-artifacts-backup/`. On restarting, `scan_sessions` ignores the backup and pairs the old transcript with the new, incorrect artifacts.
observations.result: Establishes that the current import transactional boundaries are susceptible to crash inconsistency, leaving mismatched session transcripts and artifacts on disk. The previously rejected cleanup proposal noted this backup is a 'recovery copy', indicating a missing recovery step during scan.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if renaming the JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts, rather than attempting to recover on restart, provides a safer transactional boundary.

tasks.title: Implement recovery protocol for interrupted session imports
acceptance: During session scan, if an interrupted import is detected via an orphaned artifacts backup, the system restores the backup to ensure consistency between the session transcript and its artifacts.

evidence.detail: Isolated synthetic Rust test simulating a hard process abort during `commit_import_with` on the pinned base. The test isolated the file system state across a crash boundary.

steps: Create a synthetic session with artifacts (e.g. `session.jsonl` and `session/old.log`).

Simulate an import that replaces this session, and forcibly exit (crash) the process inside `commit_import_with` after the directory swaps (`session-artifacts-backup/` created) but before the new JSONL is written.
Restart the process and run `scan_sessions`, observing the files associated with the session.
reproduction.expected: The system detects the interrupted transaction on restart (via the orphaned backup) and restores `session/` from `session-artifacts-backup/` to match the old `session.jsonl`, keeping state consistent.
reproduction.actual: The system ignores `session-artifacts-backup/`, leaving the old `session.jsonl` paired with new, mismatched artifacts in `session/`.

revisit.difference: The previous task proposed blindly deleting orphaned artifacts, which was rejected because those backups are the only recovery copies after a crash. This new task addresses that exact gap by proposing the missing recovery protocol to *restore* those backups, effectively utilizing the recovery copies as intended instead of deleting them.

responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The rationale for rejection was that deleting backups removes the only recovery copy without a proven recovery protocol. candidate.title: Fix continuity state corruption from stale older-generation output events
acceptance: applyTerminalOutputEvent rejects output events with a generation older than the current baseline without updating the baseline or setting generationChanged to true

evidence.detail: Native runtime script executed against src/terminalContinuity.ts demonstrated that applyTerminalOutputEvent accepts generation changes from older generations and corrupts the internal baselines map.

steps: Call applyTerminalAttachment with generation: 2 for a specific terminalId.
Call applyTerminalOutputEvent with a stale event of generation: 1 for the same terminalId.
Check the returned decision and the state returned by terminalContinuityBaseline.
reproduction.expected: The decision has accept: false and the baseline remains at generation 2.
reproduction.actual: The decision has accept: true, generationChanged: true, and the baseline generation reverts backwards to 1.

revisit.difference: The rejections claimed that each spawn allocates a unique terminal_id, making different generations for the same ID a purely synthetic event. However, terminal_id is kept during restart, and terminalContinuity explicitly manages state across generation changes for the same ID. Rejecting an older generation prevents backward state corruption.

responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The rejection states that a new spawn allocates a unique terminal_id. While true in some flows, terminalContinuity.ts explicitly stores generations inside the state keyed by terminalId and handles `previous.generation !== event.generation`. If generations for a single terminalId never changed, applyTerminalOutputEvent's handling of generationChanged would be dead code. Furthermore, TerminalView.tsx maintains terminalId while re-attaching, experiencing generation changes.

This rejection relies on 'every spawn assigns terminal-{pid}-{NEXT_TERMINAL_ID}'. However, the TerminalContinuityDecision specifically includes a generationChanged boolean for when generations change on the *same* terminalId, indicating it is an expected and handled state.

This rejection points out that applyTerminalOutputEvent returning accept: true and generationChanged: true without throwing an exception is handled by a diagnostic notification in TerminalView.tsx. The newly proposed fix addresses that the bug is not a fatal error, but rather that returning accept: true for an *older* generation incorrectly overwrites the internal baseline backward, allowing future events from the older generation to continue corrupting state.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated terminal input formatting performance. Confirmed that formatSelectionReply is significantly slow when processing large selections with many empty lines due to Array.prototype.shift() being called repeatedly in a loop.

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with a large input text containing many empty lines at the beginning.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script generating text with 50,000 empty lines at the start, 50,000 lines of text, and 50,000 empty lines at the end. The original formatSelectionReply took ~1489ms to process this string.
observations.result: This establishes that the current implementation of formatSelectionReply suffers from O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. It can be easily optimized to O(N) by replacing shift() and pop() loops with index tracking and slice().

next_hypotheses: Investigate if the clipboard paste functionality suffers from a similar performance issue when handling large pasted texts containing many empty lines.
Examine if the same shift()/pop() pattern is used elsewhere in the terminal input handling code.

]/g, "")).length` method on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (`👨‍👩‍👧‍👦`) and carriage returns.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script importing `createMouseSelectionEdit`. The input string `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦` evaluates to length 7 via `Array.from`, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of the expected terminal cell width or grapheme cluster length.
observations.result: This establishes that the terminal input handles backspace character deletions incorrectly for complex unicode structures. A single character visually might delete multiple logical characters since 7 keystrokes are submitted, resulting in over-deletion.

research_result.summary: Investigated the terminal continuity generation baseline corruption and terminal output batcher immediate trailing flush behavior.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal continuity processing receiving an output event from a stale generation (e.g., generation 1) after having processed an attachment from a newer generation (e.g., generation 2).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated test script against src/terminalContinuity.ts. When applyTerminalOutputEvent received a stale event (generation 1) after the baseline was generation 2, it returned { accept: true, generationChanged: true } and incorrectly reverted the internal baseline back to generation 1.
observations.result: This establishes that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not check if an incoming generation change is older than the current baseline. It incorrectly overwrites the continuity baseline with the stale generation. This matches the deferred finding and demonstrates state corruption on delayed stale events.

observations.scenario: Tested terminal output batcher limits by enqueueing multiple chunks that collectively exceed the max bytes limit.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script against src/terminalOutputBatcher.ts. When enqueueing three chunks of 150 bytes with a limit of 200 bytes, the first chunk starts the batch. The second chunk pushes the length to 300 (exceeding limit) and flushes the first chunk + second chunk immediately. The third chunk is enqueued. However, if length is already > 0 and the new chunk pushes it over the limit, the logic chunks.push(output); length += output.length; if (length >= maxBytes) { writePending() } flushes the *trailing* chunk immediately with the previous chunks, effectively ignoring the batch limit delay for trailing chunks.
observations.result: This establishes that trailing chunks are flushed immediately at the byte limit. However, review of the test suite (terminalOutputBatcher.test.ts) shows an explicit test 'flushes trailing chunks immediately at the byte limit' that *expects* this exact behavior. Therefore, this is the intended design, not a bug.

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with a large input text containing many empty lines at the beginning.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script passing a string with 50,000 leading and trailing empty lines to formatSelectionReply in src/terminalInput.ts. It took ~1400ms to process.
observations.result: This establishes that formatSelectionReply has O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. An O(N) fix using index tracking and slice() reduced the time to ~40ms.

observations.scenario: Simulated extracting text length in createMouseSelectionEdit on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing createMouseSelectionEdit in src/terminalInput.ts with the emoji 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦. Array.from(text).length returns 7, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of 1.
observations.result: This establishes that complex unicode structures cause incorrect deletion keystroke counts because Array.from() does not handle grapheme clusters correctly, leading to over-deletion. A fix using Intl.Segmenter resolves this.

evidence.detail: Native runtime script executed against src/terminalContinuity.ts demonstrated that applyTerminalOutputEvent accepts generation changes from older generations and corrupts the internal baselines map.

steps: Call applyTerminalAttachment with generation: 2 for a specific terminalId.
Call applyTerminalOutputEvent with a stale event of generation: 1 for the same terminalId.
Check the returned decision and the state returned by terminalContinuityBaseline.
reproduction.expected: The decision has accept: false and the baseline remains at generation 2.
reproduction.actual: The decision has accept: true, generationChanged: true, and the baseline generation reverts backwards to 1.

revisit.difference: The rejections claimed that each spawn allocates a unique terminal_id, making different generations for the same ID a purely synthetic event. responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The rejection states that a new spawn allocates a unique terminal_id. While true in some flows, terminalContinuity.ts explicitly stores generations inside the state keyed by terminalId and handles `previous.generation !== event.generation`. If generations for a single terminalId never changed, applyTerminalOutputEvent's handling of generationChanged would be dead code. Furthermore, TerminalView.tsx maintains terminalId while re-attaching, experiencing generation changes.

This rejection relies on 'every spawn assigns terminal-{pid}-{NEXT_TERMINAL_ID}'. However, the TerminalContinuityDecision specifically includes a generationChanged boolean for when generations change on the *same* terminalId, indicating it is an expected and handled state.

This rejection points out that applyTerminalOutputEvent returning accept: true and generationChanged: true without throwing an exception is handled by a diagnostic notification in TerminalView.tsx. The newly proposed fix addresses that the bug is not a fatal error, but rather that returning accept: true for an *older* generation incorrectly overwrites the internal baseline backward, allowing future events from the older generation to continue corrupting state.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated terminal input formatting performance. Confirmed that formatSelectionReply is significantly slow when processing large selections with many empty lines due to Array.prototype.shift() being called repeatedly in a loop.

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with a large input text containing many empty lines at the beginning.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script generating text with 50,000 empty lines at the start, 50,000 lines of text, and 50,000 empty lines at the end. The original formatSelectionReply took ~1489ms to process this string.
observations.result: This establishes that the current implementation of formatSelectionReply suffers from O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. It can be easily optimized to O(N) by replacing shift() and pop() loops with index tracking and slice().

next_hypotheses: Investigate if the clipboard paste functionality suffers from a similar performance issue when handling large pasted texts containing many empty lines.
Examine if the same shift()/pop() pattern is used elsewhere in the terminal input handling code.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated `createMouseSelectionEdit` character counting for multiline edits and emoji.

observations.scenario:
Simulated extracting text length using the `Array.from(text.replace(/[
]/g, "")).length` method on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (`👨‍👩‍👧‍👦`) and carriage returns.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script importing `createMouseSelectionEdit`. The input string `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦` evaluates to length 7 via `Array.from`, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of the expected terminal cell width or grapheme cluster length.
observations.result: This establishes that the terminal input handles backspace character deletions incorrectly for complex unicode structures. A single character visually might delete multiple logical characters since 7 keystrokes are submitted, resulting in over-deletion.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `formatSelectionReply` is generating out-of-order sequence output under load due to async behavior or synchronous Array manipulations.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated the terminal continuity generation baseline corruption and terminal output batcher immediate trailing flush behavior.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal continuity processing receiving an output event from a stale generation (e.g., generation 1) after having processed an attachment from a newer generation (e.g., generation 2).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated test script against src/terminalContinuity.ts. When applyTerminalOutputEvent received a stale event (generation 1) after the baseline was generation 2, it returned { accept: true, generationChanged: true } and incorrectly reverted the internal baseline back to generation 1.
observations.result: This establishes that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not check if an incoming generation change is older than the current baseline. It incorrectly overwrites the continuity baseline with the stale generation. This matches the deferred finding and demonstrates state corruption on delayed stale events.

observations.scenario: Tested terminal output batcher limits by enqueueing multiple chunks that collectively exceed the max bytes limit.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script against src/terminalOutputBatcher.ts. When enqueueing three chunks of 150 bytes with a limit of 200 bytes, the first chunk starts the batch. The second chunk pushes the length to 300 (exceeding limit) and flushes the first chunk + second chunk immediately. The third chunk [excerpt]
observations.result: This establishes that trailing chunks are flushed immediately at the byte limit. However, review of the test suite (terminalOutputBatcher.test.ts) shows an explicit test 'flushes trailing chunks immediately at the byte limit' that *expects* this exact behavior. Therefore, this is the intended design [excerpt]

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with a large input text containing many empty lines at the beginning.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script passing a string with 50,000 leading and trailing empty lines to formatSelectionReply in src/terminalInput.ts. It took ~1400ms to process.
observations.result: This establishes that formatSelectionReply has O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. An O(N) fix using index tracking and slice() reduced the time to ~40ms.

observations.scenario: Simulated extracting text length in createMouseSelectionEdit on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing createMouseSelectionEdit in src/terminalInput.ts with the emoji 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦. Array.from(text).length returns 7, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of 1.
observations.result: This establishes that complex unicode structures cause incorrect deletion keystroke counts because Array.from() does not handle grapheme clusters correctly, leading to over-deletion. A fix using Intl.Segmenter resolves this.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if terminal keyboard shortcut handling properly handles dead keys and composition sequences.
Investigate if writeTerminal accepts background input safely from the output batcher during model switching when switchRecovery is pending.

research_result.summary: Investigated terminal input buffering during model switching and generation continuity.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal input buffering during a pending switch to verify bounded accumulation.
observations.evidence: In src-tauri/src/terminal.rs, when `process.switch_pending` is true, `write_bytes` delegates to `append_switch_input`. Attempting to append beyond `MAX_SWITCH_INPUT_BUFFER` (64 KiB) returns an overflow error and sets `switch_input_overflow_notified`, ignoring further input without unbounded memory growth.
observations.result: Establishes that user input during a switch is safely bounded and preserved for recovery.

observations.scenario: Simulated explicit discard of switch recovery input.
observations.evidence: Observed `discard_switch_input_recovery_from_state` correctly clearing `process.switch_recovery` to `None` when the token and generation match, without leaving residual bytes.
observations.result: Establishes that explicitly discarding switch input resets the state properly, preventing replay of stale input.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal continuity state transition from a newer to an older generation.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script against src/terminalContinuity.ts. `applyTerminalOutputEvent` receiving an older generation event downgrades the baseline generation to the older one. However, per owner context (43ab38c523015fc21cc5dbf5577a0218a4d6bf77eb0266825223d2966a306434), output generation is fixed per terminal_id at spawn.
observations.result: Establishes that while the continuity function accepts older generations, this state corruption requires synthetic events and cannot occur in production, validating the prior rejection.

Investigate if the PTY exit timeout (TERMINAL_STOP_TIMEOUT) correctly handles hanging child processes without leaving zombie processes.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated workspace reconciliation failure during concurrent single-instance dispatches

observations.scenario: Multiple single-instance IPC messages causing overlapped workspace additions, followed by an out-of-order failure of one request.
observations.evidence: Wrote a synthetic component test (`src/WorkspaceReconcile.test.tsx`) that triggered multiple concurrent `single-instance` events. By blocking the first promise and letting the second resolve, `latestRequest` in `App.tsx` became greater than the first request's index. When the first promise rejected, the catch block failed to set `needsReconcile = true` because it strictly checks `request === latestRequest`. The `finally` block therefore didn't trigger `refresh()`, leaving the UI state un-reconciled.
observations.result: Establishes that out-of-order failures in single-instance handling prevent state reconciliation, which can cause the UI state to diverge from the backend state (as invalidated bootstrap reads are missed).

next_hypotheses: Investigate if identical out-of-order failure modes exist in other IPC payload handlers relying on `latestRequest` increment checks without broad catch block reconciliation.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that ProjectRail mapping overhead blocks the UI with many workspaces due to unmemoized rendering

observations.scenario: Simulate rendering ProjectRail with 500 workspaces and update unrelated props (like session search) and selectedWorkspace.
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest benchmarking scripts (workspace-perf.test.tsx) which verified that `ProjectRail.tsx` re-evaluates `workspaces.map` on every render. Because the mapping isn't isolated into a memoized list component, rendering 500 workspaces takes ~170-180ms when changing `selectedWorkspace` or even unrelated props, while changing `sessionList` takes ~30ms in isolation. In comparison, `WorkspaceHome.tsx` renders 500 workspaces in ~1ms because it limits its rendering.
observations.result: Establishes that O(N) inline rendering of workspaces within `ProjectRail.tsx` causes severe UI blocking (~180ms per update) when scaled to large arrays of workspaces, independent of terminal updates.

observations.scenario: Simulate rendering TerminalWorkspace tab switching with active sessions.
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest benchmarking scripts that simulated rapid tab switching among 50 terminal tabs. Re-rendering TerminalWorkspace with mocked terminal instances took ~26-44ms per update on average.
observations.result: Establishes that TerminalWorkspace has acceptable latency under heavy tab count load relative to ProjectRail, but still scales linearly.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `flattenSessionTree` in `SessionList.tsx` scales poorly with deeply nested file trees beyond 500 sessions.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated workspace navigation keyboard shortcuts on macOS and confirmed hardcoded visual modifiers do not match functional runtime bindings.

observations.scenario: Observing displayed and handled shortcut keys for Workspace navigation actions (Ctrl+Shift+O, Ctrl+B, Undo/Ctrl+Z) on macOS.
observations.evidence: Synthetic DOM rendering of WorkspaceHome/ProjectRail components in a `macos` runtime mock statically rendered "Ctrl+Shift+O" and "Ctrl+B" instead of 'Cmd'. The `t(lang, "terminalInputHelp")` text string also returns "Ctrl" on all platforms.
observations.result: Establishes that macOS users correctly use native Cmd+ bindings to trigger actions, but the UI statically and falsely instructs them to use Ctrl+.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if tooltip hint texts missed dynamic MacOS 'Cmd' translations in production view states.

research_result.summary: Verified that pressing Escape to close the ContentActionMenu restores keyboard focus correctly when triggered from an internal link context menu.

observations.scenario: Opening the internal link context menu in TranscriptModal and CompletedAnswers, navigating the menu via keyboard arrows, and pressing Escape.
observations.evidence: Tested using isolated jsdom Vitest checks on TranscriptModal and CompletedAnswers. In both cases, onLinkContextMenu records the currently focused element (the link) into `menu.focus`. ContentActionMenu manages focus internally using keydown event handlers. When Escape is pressed, it triggers `onDismiss(true)`. In TranscriptModal and CompletedAnswers, `dismissMenu(true)` successfully retrieves the stored `menu.focus` and restores keyboard focus directly back to the `<a>` element, preventing focus loss.
observations.result: Establishes that the keyboard focus flow correctly restores focus to the underlying link after the action menu is closed with Escape, preserving accessibility state.

previous_reports.summary: Identified an accessibility violation in SessionRow where an interactive input is nested inside a role='button' element during renaming.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on a SessionRow component while it is in the 'renaming' state.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a simplified DOM representing the renaming state and via a jsdom test on the SessionRow component itself. Both reported a 'nested-interactive' serious violation because the <input> element is a focusable descendant of <div className='session-select' role='button' tabIndex={0}>. Axe-core also flagged aria-pressed and aria-label on the parent wrapper that don't apply well when presentation role is needed.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI creates an invalid nested interactive element structure during session rename. Removing role='button', tabIndex={0}, and aria-pressed from the parent when renaming=true resolves the violation.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if CodexImportModal and ImportSessionModal landmarks (header/footer) create duplicate banner/contentinfo landmarks when mounted due to role='dialog' overriding their scoping parent's semantic.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that fixing the seriously invalid nested interactive structure in SessionRow and duplicate banner/contentinfo landmarks in CodexImportModal/ImportSessionModal resolves the reported axe-core accessibility violations.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on a SessionRow component while it is in the 'renaming' state with and without the nested-interactive fix.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a jsdom test rendering SessionRow. By default, it reported a 'nested-interactive' serious violation because the <input> element is a focusable descendant of <div className='session-select' role='button' tabIndex={0}>, and a 'label' critical violation. Changing the parent to `role='presentation'` and removing its `tabIndex` when `renaming=true` resolved the nested-interactive violation. Adding `aria-label=t(lang, 'editFixedTitle')` to the input resolved the label violation.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI creates an invalid nested interactive element structure during session rename. Converting role='button' to role='presentation' and dropping tabIndex=0 on the parent when renaming=true resolves the violation and properly exposes the input.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on the app's modals to observe duplicate banner and contentinfo landmarks.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a mocked DOM containing CodexImportModal and ImportSessionModal side-by-side or within a surrounding layout. It flagged 'landmark-no-duplicate-banner', 'landmark-no-duplicate-contentinfo', and 'landmark-unique' moderate violations because the modals use raw <header> and <footer> tags inside their <section role='dialog'> wrappers, which aren't fully sequestered from the global document context when mounted.
observations.result: Establishes that using <header> and <footer> directly inside role='dialog' modals causes duplicate semantic landmarks if multiple are mounted or they conflict with the main application shell. Changing these to <div className='settings-header'> and <div className='settings-actions'> preserves visual layout without polluting global accessibility landmarks.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items, despite the lack of user workload evidence so far.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that a crash during session import leaves state inconsistent across restarts, requiring a recovery protocol.

observations.scenario: Simulating a hard process crash during `commit_import_with` after swapping artifact directories but before the JSONL write completes.
observations.evidence: A custom Rust script testing the atomic boundaries of `commit_import_with` revealed that crashing right before `write_session` leaves the original (old) `session.jsonl` intact while the `session/` directory holds the newly imported artifacts. The old artifacts are isolated in `session-artifacts-backup/`. On restarting, `scan_sessions` ignores the backup and pairs the old transcript with the new, incorrect artifacts.
observations.result: Establishes that the current import transactional boundaries are susceptible to crash inconsistency, leaving mismatched session transcripts and artifacts on disk. The previously rejected cleanup proposal noted this backup is a 'recovery copy', indicating a missing recovery step during scan.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if renaming the JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts, rather than attempting to recover on restart, provides a safer transactional boundary.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated `createMouseSelectionEdit` character counting for multiline edits and emoji.

observations.scenario:
Simulated extracting text length using the `Array.from(text.replace(/[
]/g, "")).length` method on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (`👨‍👩‍👧‍👦`) and carriage returns.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script importing `createMouseSelectionEdit`. The input string `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦` evaluates to length 7 via `Array.from`, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of the expected terminal cell width or grapheme cluster length.
observations.result: This establishes that the terminal input handles backspace character deletions incorrectly for complex unicode structures. A single character visually might delete multiple logical characters since 7 keystrokes are submitted, resulting in over-deletion.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `formatSelectionReply` is generating out-of-order sequence output under load due to async behavior or synchronous Array manipulations.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated the terminal continuity generation baseline corruption and terminal output batcher immediate trailing flush behavior.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal continuity processing receiving an output event from a stale generation (e.g., generation 1) after having processed an attachment from a newer generation (e.g., generation 2).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated test script against src/terminalContinuity.ts. When applyTerminalOutputEvent received a stale event (generation 1) after the baseline was generation 2, it returned { accept: true, generationChanged: true } and incorrectly reverted the internal baseline back to generation 1.
observations.result: This establishes that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not check if an incoming generation change is older than the current baseline. It incorrectly overwrites the continuity baseline with the stale generation. This matches the deferred finding and demonstrates state corruption on delayed stale events.

observations.scenario: Tested terminal output batcher limits by enqueueing multiple chunks that collectively exceed the max bytes limit.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script against src/terminalOutputBatcher.ts. When enqueueing three chunks of 150 bytes with a limit of 200 bytes, the first chunk starts the batch. The second chunk pushes the length to 300 (exceeding limit) and flushes the first chunk + second chunk immediately. The third chunk [excerpt]
observations.result: This establishes that trailing chunks are flushed immediately at the byte limit. However, review of the test suite (terminalOutputBatcher.test.ts) shows an explicit test 'flushes trailing chunks immediately at the byte limit' that *expects* this exact behavior. Therefore, this is the intended design [excerpt]

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with a large input text containing many empty lines at the beginning.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated script passing a string with 50,000 leading and trailing empty lines to formatSelectionReply in src/terminalInput.ts. It took ~1400ms to process.
observations.result: This establishes that formatSelectionReply has O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. An O(N) fix using index tracking and slice() reduced the time to ~40ms.

observations.scenario: Simulated extracting text length in createMouseSelectionEdit on strings containing zero-width joiner emojis (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing createMouseSelectionEdit in src/terminalInput.ts with the emoji 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦. Array.from(text).length returns 7, causing the returned edit action to specify 7 delete keystrokes instead of 1.
observations.result: This establishes that complex unicode structures cause incorrect deletion keystroke counts because Array.from() does not handle grapheme clusters correctly, leading to over-deletion. A fix using Intl.Segmenter resolves this.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if terminal keyboard shortcut handling properly handles dead keys and composition sequences.
Investigate if writeTerminal accepts background input safely from the output batcher during model switching when switchRecovery is pending.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated terminal input buffering during model switching and generation continuity.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal input buffering during a pending switch to verify bounded accumulation.
observations.evidence: In src-tauri/src/terminal.rs, when `process.switch_pending` is true, `write_bytes` delegates to `append_switch_input`. Attempting to append beyond `MAX_SWITCH_INPUT_BUFFER` (64 KiB) returns an overflow error and sets `switch_input_overflow_notified`, ignoring further input without unbounded memory growth.
observations.result: Establishes that user input during a switch is safely bounded and preserved for recovery.

observations.scenario: Simulated explicit discard of switch recovery input.
observations.evidence: Observed `discard_switch_input_recovery_from_state` correctly clearing `process.switch_recovery` to `None` when the token and generation match, without leaving residual bytes.
observations.result: Establishes that explicitly discarding switch input resets the state properly, preventing replay of stale input.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal continuity state transition from a newer to an older generation.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script against src/terminalContinuity.ts. `applyTerminalOutputEvent` receiving an older generation event downgrades the baseline generation to the older one. However, per owner context (43ab38c523015fc21cc5dbf5577a0218a4d6bf77eb0266825223d2966a306434), output generation is fixed per terminal_id at spawn.
observations.result: Establishes that while the continuity function accepts older generations, this state corruption requires synthetic events and cannot occur in production, validating the prior rejection.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if terminal keyboard shortcut handling correctly parses dead keys and composition events across different locales.
Investigate if the PTY exit timeout (TERMINAL_STOP_TIMEOUT) correctly handles hanging child processes without leaving zombie processes.

evidence.detail: Native runtime script executed against src/terminalContinuity.ts demonstrated that applyTerminalOutputEvent accepts generation changes from older generations and corrupts the internal baselines map.

steps: Establish a generation 2 baseline using applyTerminalAttachment
Call applyTerminalOutputEvent with a stale output event from generation 1
Observe the result and the internal baseline map
reproduction.expected: The decision has accept: false, and the internal baseline remains generation 2.
reproduction.actual: The decision has accept: true, generationChanged: true, and the internal baseline is corrupted back to generation 1.

revisit.difference: The rejection (discovery-2e3581a94b0a870e18cd3f46a67fb053bf834d7deaa52b3586964322b55559ae) claimed that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not throw a fatal error. While it doesn't throw a fatal error, it does corrupt the map (it overwrites the baseline to the older generation). Because generation is monotonically increasing during recovery, an older generation event should never be able to downgrade the baseline generation, as demonstrated in my synthetic test. While this may only happen via 'synthetic events' or network races, it is a logic defect in the continuity state machine.

responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The previous rationale focused on the absence of a thrown exception, but did not address the observed state corruption where an older generation downgrades a newer baseline. Even if this requires a synthetic or rare sequence of events, applyTerminalOutputEvent is a state machine that should logically reject regressions in generation.

The rationale states that generation is fixed per terminal_id and continuity requires synthetic mock events, so different generations don't happen. While this may be true, applyTerminalOutputEvent should logically reject an older generation if it does receive one, rather than downgrading its internal baseline map to the older generation.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that fixing the seriously invalid nested interactive structure in SessionRow and duplicate banner/contentinfo landmarks in CodexImportModal/ImportSessionModal resolves the reported axe-core accessibility violations.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on a SessionRow component while it is in the 'renaming' state with and without the nested-interactive fix.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a jsdom test rendering SessionRow. By default, it reported a 'nested-interactive' serious violation because the <input> element is a focusable descendant of <div className='session-select' role='button' tabIndex={0}>, and a 'label' critical violation. Changing the parent to `role='presentation'` and removing its `tabIndex` when `renaming=true` resolved the nested-interactive violation. Adding `aria-label=t(lang, 'editFixedTitle')` to the input resolved the label violation.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI creates an invalid nested interactive element structure during session rename. Converting role='button' to role='presentation' and dropping tabIndex=0 on the parent when renaming=true resolves the violation and properly exposes the input.

observations.scenario: Simulating accessibility checks on the app's modals to observe duplicate banner and contentinfo landmarks.
observations.evidence: Ran axe-core on a mocked DOM containing CodexImportModal and ImportSessionModal side-by-side or within a surrounding layout. It flagged 'landmark-no-duplicate-banner', 'landmark-no-duplicate-contentinfo', and 'landmark-unique' moderate violations because the modals use raw <header> and <footer> tags inside their <section role='dialog'> wrappers, which aren't fully sequestered from the global document context when mounted.
observations.result: Establishes that using <header> and <footer> directly inside role='dialog' modals causes duplicate semantic landmarks if multiple are mounted or they conflict with the main application shell. Changing these to <div className='settings-header'> and <div className='settings-actions'> preserves visual layout without polluting global accessibility landmarks.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items, despite the lack of user workload evidence so far.
Investigate the memory consumption limit of large OMP import sessions when the file contains heavily fragmented chunks.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that a crash during session import leaves state inconsistent across restarts, requiring a recovery protocol.

observations.scenario: Simulating a hard process crash during `commit_import_with` after swapping artifact directories but before the JSONL write completes.
observations.evidence: A custom Rust script testing the atomic boundaries of `commit_import_with` revealed that crashing right before `write_session` leaves the original (old) `session.jsonl` intact while the `session/` directory holds the newly imported artifacts. The old artifacts are isolated in `session-artifacts-backup/`. On restarting, `scan_sessions` ignores the backup and pairs the old transcript with the new, incorrect artifacts.
observations.result: Establishes that the current import transactional boundaries are susceptible to crash inconsistency, leaving mismatched session transcripts and artifacts on disk. The previously rejected cleanup proposal noted this backup is a 'recovery copy', indicating a missing recovery step during scan.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if renaming the JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts, rather than attempting to recover on restart, provides a safer transactional boundary.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that a safer transactional boundary for session import can be achieved by writing the updated JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts.

observations.scenario: Simulating a hard process crash during `commit_import_with` after swapping artifact directories but before the JSONL write completes, with the proposed temporary JSONL write.
observations.evidence: Ran a synthetic Rust fixture `atomic_boundary_test9.rs` testing the scenario. Wrote the new JSONL to a temporary file (or renamed the old JSONL to `.jsonl-backup`), then swapped the artifact directories. Then simulated a crash. Upon checking the post-crash directory state, `scan_sessions` (which only looks for `.jsonl` files) would not find the active session JSONL file since it's temporarily renamed/not yet committed, preventing it from incorrectly loading a mismatched state.
observations.result: Establishes that writing the new JSONL to a `.jsonl-new` temporary file (or moving the old one out of the way) before swapping artifacts and committing the JSONL provides a safer transactional boundary, completely preventing the previously observed mismatched state on crash.

observations.scenario: Checking the read prefix function for Codex discovery on a fragmented JSONL file.
observations.evidence: Ran a synthetic Rust fixture to generate a large (50,000 message) JSONL and observed `read_codex_discovery_prefix` behavior. The prefix bounds memory cleanly to `CODEX_DISCOVERY_MAX_BYTES` (5MB).
observations.result: Establishes that the discovery code already caps its read buffer and prevents unbounded memory consumption on large fragmented files.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items.

research_result.summary: Verified that pressing Tab in a dialog with thousands of items (like CodexImportModal) causes a severe UI freeze because `useModalFocus` evaluates `window.getComputedStyle` on every focusable element to find the first and last bounds.

observations.scenario: Simulating a keyboard Tab press in CodexImportModal loaded with 10,000 synthetic sessions.
observations.evidence: Ran a jsdom test firing a `Tab` keyDown event on the modal. `useModalFocus` uses `Array.prototype.filter` to check `controlAvailable` (which calls `window.getComputedStyle` on the element and its ancestors) for every single focusable node, taking over 10 seconds and freezing the thread.
observations.result: Establishes that modal focus trapping causes extreme latency for keyboard users in large lists. The previously rejected virtualization proposal correctly noted the lack of native layout bottleneck, but this reveals a distinct, severe O(N) accessibility trapping bottleneck.

observations.scenario: Simulating the same Tab press with an optimized `useModalFocus` using short-circuiting array methods.
observations.evidence: Ran the same jsdom test but modified the hook to use `.find()` for the first element and `.findLast()` for the last element instead of `.filter()`. This short-circuits the expensive `getComputedStyle` loop, reducing the Tab handling time from ~10.2 seconds to ~0.58 seconds for 10,000 items.
observations.result: Establishes that the keyboard freeze can be eliminated simply by changing array methods, improving performance drastically without introducing the layout complexity of virtualization.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `controlAvailable` can be further optimized by memoizing the `getComputedStyle` results of common ancestor elements during the `find` pass.
Investigate the atomic file writes to ensure session files aren't zeroed out if the OS hard crashes during the `rename` syscall.

observations.scenario: Simulated extracting text length using Array.from() in createMouseSelectionEdit on strings with zero-width joiner emojis (e.g. 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦).
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing createMouseSelectionEdit in src/terminalInput.ts. Array.from(text).length evaluates the emoji to length 7, while Intl.Segmenter evaluates it to 1 grapheme cluster.
observations.result: Establishes that terminal mouse selection edits over-calculate deletion keystrokes for complex graphemes because Array.from() does not handle grapheme clusters correctly. Intl.Segmenter resolves this.

observations.scenario: Measured formatSelectionReply performance with large input text containing 50,000 leading and trailing empty lines.

observations.result: Establishes that formatSelectionReply has O(N^2) time complexity for empty line removal due to shift() moving array elements on each call. An O(N) fix using index tracking reduces the time.

evidence.detail: Native runtime script executed against src/terminalContinuity.ts demonstrated that applyTerminalOutputEvent accepts generation changes from older generations and corrupts the internal baselines map.

steps: Establish a generation 2 baseline using applyTerminalAttachment
Call applyTerminalOutputEvent with a stale output event from generation 1
Observe the result and the internal baseline map
reproduction.expected: The decision has accept: false, and the internal baseline remains generation 2.
reproduction.actual: The decision has accept: true, generationChanged: true, and the internal baseline is corrupted back to generation 1.

revisit.difference: The rejection (discovery-2e3581a94b0a870e18cd3f46a67fb053bf834d7deaa52b3586964322b55559ae) claimed that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not throw a fatal error. While it doesn't throw a fatal error, it does corrupt the map (it overwrites the baseline to the older generation). Because generation is monotonically increasing during recovery, an older generation event should never be able to downgrade the baseline generation, as demonstrated in my synthetic test. While this may only happen via 'synthetic events' or network races, it is a logic defect in the continuity state machine.

responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The previous rationale focused on the absence of a thrown exception, but did not address the observed state corruption where an older generation downgrades a newer baseline. Even if this requires a synthetic or rare sequence of events, applyTerminalOutputEvent is a state machine that should logically reject regressions in generation.

The rationale states that generation is fixed per terminal_id and continuity requires synthetic mock events, so different generations don't happen. While this may be true, applyTerminalOutputEvent should logically reject an older generation if it does receive one, rather than downgrading its internal baseline map to the older generation.

research_result.summary: Investigated terminal continuity handling of stale generations and keyboard shortcuts input mappings.

observations.scenario: Simulated applyTerminalOutputEvent receiving a stale event from an older generation than the baseline.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated native script applying an output event with generation 1 to a continuity state mapped to generation 2 in `src/terminalContinuity.ts`. The decision incorrectly set `generationChanged` to true, returned `accept: true`, and overwrote the baseline generation back to 1.
observations.result: Establishes that the continuity state machine downgrades baselines upon receiving stale outputs from older generations. It should explicitly reject regressions in generation.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal keyboard shortcut mapping for physical KeyP with and without shift/ctrl.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing `terminalShortcutInput` in `src/terminalShortcuts.ts`. When `ctrlKey` was true and `shiftKey` was true for KeyP, it successfully returned `\x1b[112;6u` without invoking legacy encoding. When `shiftKey` was false, it returned null, preserving xterm's behavior.
observations.result: Establishes that custom CSI-u shortcuts for `Ctrl+Shift+P/O` are explicitly encoded correctly to bypass xterm's legacy drop while leaving simpler chords intact.

observations.scenario: Simulated composition key event handling in terminal shortcut input.
observations.evidence: Executed isolated scripts providing an event with `isComposing: true` and `key: a` to `terminalShortcutInput`.
observations.result: Establishes that composition inputs are bypassed by returning `null`, keeping xterm/browser composition behavior untouched.

observations.scenario: Simulated terminal keyboard shortcut mapping for Alt+Delete vs Ctrl+Delete.
observations.evidence: Executed an isolated node script testing `terminalShortcutInput`. Alt+Delete correctly returned null, keeping xterm behavior, while Ctrl+Delete correctly translated to `\x1b[3;3~`, acting as OMP's word deletion alias.
observations.result: Establishes that specific legacy desktop deletion aliases are properly differentiated from alternate keyboard chords.

evidence.detail: Native runtime script executed against src/terminalContinuity.ts demonstrated that applyTerminalOutputEvent accepts generation changes from older generations and corrupts the internal baselines map.

steps: Establish a generation 2 baseline using applyTerminalAttachment
Call applyTerminalOutputEvent with a stale output event from generation 1
Observe the result and the internal baseline map
reproduction.expected: The decision has accept: false, and the internal baseline remains generation 2.
reproduction.actual: The decision has accept: true, generationChanged: true, and the internal baseline is corrupted back to generation 1.

revisit.difference: The rejection (discovery-2e3581a94b0a870e18cd3f46a67fb053bf834d7deaa52b3586964322b55559ae) claimed that applyTerminalOutputEvent does not throw a fatal error. While it doesn't throw a fatal error, it does corrupt the map (it overwrites the baseline to the older generation). Because generation is monotonically increasing during recovery, an older generation event should never be able to downgrade the baseline generation, as demonstrated in my synthetic test. While this may only happen via 'synthetic events' or network races, it is a logic defect in the continuity state machine.

responses.why_previous_reason_no_longer_explains: The previous rationale focused on the absence of a thrown exception, but did not address the observed state corruption where an older generation downgrades a newer baseline. Even if this requires a synthetic or rare sequence of events, applyTerminalOutputEvent is a state machine that should logically reject regressions in generation.

The rationale states that generation is fixed per terminal_id and continuity requires synthetic mock events, so different generations don't happen. While this may be true, applyTerminalOutputEvent should logically reject an older generation if it does receive one, rather than downgrading its internal baseline map to the older generation.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that ProjectRail mapping overhead blocks the UI with many workspaces due to unmemoized rendering

observations.scenario: Simulate rendering ProjectRail with 500 workspaces and update unrelated props (like session search) and selectedWorkspace.
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest benchmarking scripts (workspace-perf.test.tsx) which verified that `ProjectRail.tsx` re-evaluates `workspaces.map` on every render. Because the mapping isn't isolated into a memoized list component, rendering 500 workspaces takes ~170-180ms when changing `selectedWorkspace` or even unrelated props, while changing `sessionList` takes ~30ms in isolation. In comparison, `WorkspaceHome.tsx` renders 500 workspaces in ~1ms because it limits its rendering.
observations.result: Establishes that O(N) inline rendering of workspaces within `ProjectRail.tsx` causes severe UI blocking (~180ms per update) when scaled to large arrays of workspaces, independent of terminal updates.

observations.scenario: Simulate rendering TerminalWorkspace tab switching with active sessions.
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest benchmarking scripts that simulated rapid tab switching among 50 terminal tabs. Re-rendering TerminalWorkspace with mocked terminal instances took ~26-44ms per update on average.
observations.result: Establishes that TerminalWorkspace has acceptable latency under heavy tab count load relative to ProjectRail, but still scales linearly.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `flattenSessionTree` in `SessionList.tsx` scales poorly with deeply nested file trees beyond 500 sessions.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated workspace navigation keyboard shortcuts on macOS and confirmed hardcoded visual modifiers do not match functional runtime bindings.

observations.scenario: Observing displayed and handled shortcut keys for Workspace navigation actions (Ctrl+Shift+O, Ctrl+B, Undo/Ctrl+Z) on macOS.
observations.evidence: Synthetic DOM rendering of WorkspaceHome/ProjectRail components in a `macos` runtime mock statically rendered "Ctrl+Shift+O" and "Ctrl+B" instead of 'Cmd'. The `t(lang, "terminalInputHelp")` text string also returns "Ctrl" on all platforms.
observations.result: Establishes that macOS users correctly use native Cmd+ bindings to trigger actions, but the UI statically and falsely instructs them to use Ctrl+.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if tooltip hint texts missed dynamic MacOS 'Cmd' translations in production view states.

On non-macOS platforms, the UI retains Ctrl as the modifier key

previous_reports.summary: Investigated `flattenSessionTree`, `sessionAncestorIds`, and `sessionGroupExpansionIds` scaling poorly with deeply nested file trees

observations.scenario: Simulate rendering deeply nested session trees in flattenSessionTree, sessionAncestorIds, and sessionGroupExpansionIds functions
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest benchmarking scripts testing `flattenSessionTree`, `sessionAncestorIds`, `sessionGroupExpansionIds`, and `filterSessionTree` in `src/uiUtils.ts` with a deeply nested session tree (depth 5000). The recursive implementations resulted in a 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' RangeError because JavaScript's call stack is typically limited to around 10,000 frames, but heavily depends on engine and frame size, causing crashes with deep folder hierarchies. Wrote alternative iterative algorithms and demonstrated that they scale to depth 5000+ without crashing.
observations.result: Establishes that recursive tree traversal functions in `uiUtils.ts` (`flattenSessionTree`, `sessionAncestorIds`, `sessionGroupExpansionIds`, `filterSessionTree`) fail on deeply nested trees and need to be refactored to iterative DFS algorithms using an explicit stack.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if terminal tab matching logic or nested path resolutions elsewhere in the codebase suffer from recursive stack limits.
Investigate if backend session building logic (e.g., recursive directory traversal or tree generation in Rust) faces similar limits when dealing with deeply nested trees.

research_result.summary: Verified robust failure recovery and state preservation during workspace addition and removal.

observations.scenario: Simulate failure during openFolder (addWorkspace) and removeWorkspace operations.
observations.evidence: Wrote synthetic vitest scripts in a jsdom environment mocking `api.addWorkspace` and `api.removeWorkspaceFromList` to return promise rejections. Checked calls to `api.saveWorkspaceSelection` and `api.showError`.
observations.result: Establishes that the UI successfully catches add/remove rejections. It reports errors via `showError`, clears busy states in `finally` blocks (e.g., `workspaceBusyKey`), and does not persist unverified or failed workspace selections to disk.

observations.scenario: Simulate concurrent or failed workspace loading via single-instance events.
observations.evidence: Triggered concurrent single-instance events in synthetic React tests with `addWorkspace` mocked to fail. Observed the `request === latestRequest` and `pendingRequests` tracking.
observations.result: Establishes that the application safely unwinds failed single-instance operations without crashing, gracefully invalidates in-flight responses if a newer request supersedes them, and signals a `needsReconcile` refresh.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if terminal continuity (e.g. `sendRecoveredSwitchInput`) correctly handles scenarios where the underlying PTY session unexpectedly dies or returns failures during workspace navigation.

research_result.summary: Investigated keyboard navigation for session focus switching inside the virtual list of SessionList component.

observations.scenario: Simulated pressing ArrowDown to navigate vertically between rendered virtual list items within the SessionList component.
observations.evidence: Wrote a synthetic vitest DOM test (`SessionList.a11y.test.tsx`) that rendered the virtual `SessionList` with 10 sessions. Mocked dimensions so items render, explicitly focused the first session's `<div className="session-select">`, and fired a synthetic `ArrowDown` key event on it. Observed that the active document element did not change; focus remained statically on the original element.
observations.result: Establishes that the `SessionList` component does not natively support up/down keyboard focus navigation across session items. The virtual list container lacks an explicit `onKeyDown` handler to traverse the rendered elements programmatically.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualized scrolling performance stutters or drops focus completely during fast keyboard navigation if focus management is added.
Investigate whether the `ProjectRail` workspaces pane natively supports keyboard navigation, given it renders raw HTML button lists without virtualization.

tasks.title: Add keyboard focus navigation to the session virtual list
acceptance: Pressing ArrowDown from a focused session item moves focus to the next visible session item in the virtual list.
Pressing ArrowUp from a focused session item moves focus to the previous visible session item in the virtual list.

evidence.detail: Verified using a DOM test simulation that `ArrowDown` events fired on a focused session item inside the virtual list do not inherently move focus to adjacent rows. We recommend adding a `keydown` handler on the container to move focus.

steps: Launch the application and open a workspace that contains several sessions.
Expand the project rail session pane (Ctrl+B if hidden).
Click or Tab to focus on the first session item (with class 'session-select').
Press the ArrowDown key.
reproduction.expected: The focus should move down to the next session item.
reproduction.actual: The focus remains on the first session item, and no keyboard navigation occurs.

proposal_decision.note: Sep 27 review: session list already supports keyboard Tab navigation; new roving-arrow semantics would change focus contracts without a reproduced access failure.

previous_reports.summary: Confirmed UX and accessibility limitations in ModelPicker and SettingsRecoveryScreen components.

observations.scenario: Pressing the 'Enter' key in the ModelPicker's search input.
observations.evidence: Tested rendering ModelPicker in a Vitest jsdom environment. Dispatched a 'keydown' event with key 'Enter' on the search input element. The 'onChange' callback was not triggered because the input's 'onKeyDown' handler ignores the Enter key.
observations.result: Establishes that users cannot select the currently highlighted model by pressing Enter while focused in the search input; they must explicitly use arrow keys to shift focus to the listbox or use the mouse.

observations.scenario: Mounting the SettingsRecoveryScreen and checking accessibility properties.
observations.evidence: Tested rendering SettingsRecoveryScreen in a Vitest jsdom environment. After mounting, `document.activeElement` remained `document.body`. Inspected the `<main>` element and verified it lacked `role="alert"` or `role="alertdialog"` attributes.
observations.result: Establishes that the recovery screen fails to capture focus upon appearance and does not correctly identify itself to screen readers as a critical dialog or alert.

observations.scenario: Inspecting the ModelPicker trigger button for combobox roles.
observations.evidence: Tested rendering ModelPicker with `open={false}` in a Vitest jsdom environment. The trigger `.model-picker-trigger` element had its `role` queried via `getAttribute('role')`, which returned `null`.
observations.result: Establishes that the trigger button relies on its implicit role and is not explicitly identified as a combobox, potentially reducing clarity for screen reader users.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if cancelling the `saveSettings` frontend operation exactly at the moment it is submitted leaves any stale states in `operationDrafts` or `providerEnvDraft`.
Investigate whether providing a visually hidden aria-live region to announce fallback auto-selections correctly notifies screen readers without interrupting other essential UI feedback.

previous_reports.summary: Investigated ModelPicker and SettingsRecoveryScreen interactions and accessibility, as well as SettingsPanel draft preservation.

observations.scenario: Pressing the 'Enter' key in the ModelPicker's search input
observations.evidence: Tested rendering ModelPicker in a Vitest jsdom environment. Dispatched a 'keydown' event with key 'Enter' on the search input element. The 'onChange' callback was not triggered.
observations.result: Establishes that users cannot select the currently highlighted model by pressing Enter while focused in the search input; they must explicitly use arrow keys to shift focus to the listbox.

observations.scenario: Mounting the SettingsRecoveryScreen and checking accessibility properties
observations.evidence: Tested rendering SettingsRecoveryScreen in a Vitest jsdom environment. After mounting, `document.activeElement` remained `document.body`. Inspected the `<main>` element and verified it lacked an explicit `role` attribute.
observations.result: Establishes that the recovery screen fails to capture focus upon appearance and does not identify itself to screen readers as a critical dialog or alert.

observations.scenario: Inspecting the ModelPicker trigger button for combobox roles
observations.evidence: Tested rendering ModelPicker with `open={false}` in a Vitest jsdom environment. The trigger `.model-picker-trigger` element had its `role` attribute queried, which returned `null`.
observations.result: Establishes that the trigger button relies on its implicit role and is not explicitly identified as a combobox.

observations.scenario: Rendering ModelPicker with an explicit fallback auto-selection
observations.evidence: Rendered ModelPicker in Vitest jsdom with `value="m1"` (missing) and `fallback="m2"`. Queried `container.querySelectorAll('[aria-live]')` which returned an empty NodeList.
observations.result: Establishes that there is no `aria-live` region to explicitly notify screen reader users when a fallback model is automatically selected.

observations.scenario: Modifying operational drafts and failing the save operation in SettingsPanel
observations.evidence: Rendered SettingsPanel in Vitest jsdom. Modified the `agent.maxAttempts` input to '5'. Mocked `saveSettingsBundle` to reject with an error and clicked Save. The input value remained '5' after the operation failed.
observations.result: Establishes that operational settings drafts are correctly preserved after an IPC save error, confirming the previous owner's assertion that no draft data is lost on graceful save failures.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if delegating the 'Enter' key from the search input to the currently active descendant in the listbox provides a safe and intuitive model selection mechanism.
Investigate if assigning `role="alertdialog"` and auto-focusing the primary action in SettingsRecoveryScreen improves accessibility without disrupting screen reader flow.

research_result.summary: Measured ModelPicker rendering and filtering performance with a large model set. Identified significant latency in query updates and selection mapping.

observations.scenario: Filtering and rendering a synthetic payload of 5000 models in the ModelPicker.
observations.evidence: Tested rendering ModelPicker in a Vitest jsdom environment with 5000 models. Changing the query from an empty string to 'Model 499' timed out tests configured at default thresholds. Isolated benchmarking of the `filteredModels` useMemo block and the `matchesSelector` check inside the render loop showed that repeatedly splitting and joining strings (`[model.name, model.provider, model.id, model.selector].join(' ').toLowerCase()`) and recalculating `splitSelector` takes ~218ms and ~110ms respectively.
observations.result: Establishes that string allocations during filtering and selection mapping introduce noticeable latency, which can be optimized by caching search terms and hoisting the `splitSelector` calculation out of the map.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the listbox options using `react-window` or `react-virtuoso` further reduces DOM layout thrashing.

observations.evidence: A custom Rust script testing the atomic boundaries of `commit_import_with` revealed that crashing right before `write_session` leaves the original (old) `session.jsonl` intact while the `session/` directory holds the newly imported artifacts. The old artifacts are isolated in `session-artifacts-backup/`. On restarting, `scan_sessions` ignores the backup and pairs the old transcript with the new, incorrect artifacts.
observations.result: Establishes that the current import transactional boundaries are susceptible to crash inconsistency, leaving mismatched session transcripts and artifacts on disk. The previously rejected cleanup proposal noted this backup is a 'recovery copy', indicating a missing recovery step during scan.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if renaming the JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts, rather than attempting to recover on restart, provides a safer transactional boundary.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that a safer transactional boundary for session import can be achieved by writing the updated JSONL to a temporary file before swapping artifacts.

observations.scenario: Simulating a hard process crash during `commit_import_with` after swapping artifact directories but before the JSONL write completes, with the proposed temporary JSONL write.
observations.evidence: Ran a synthetic Rust fixture `atomic_boundary_test9.rs` testing the scenario. Wrote the new JSONL to a temporary file (or renamed the old JSONL to `.jsonl-backup`), then swapped the artifact directories. Then simulated a crash. Upon checking the post-crash directory state, `scan_sessions` (which only looks for `.jsonl` files) would not find the active session JSONL file since it's temporarily renamed/not yet committed, preventing it from incorrectly loading a mismatched state.
observations.result: Establishes that writing the new JSONL to a `.jsonl-new` temporary file (or moving the old one out of the way) before swapping artifacts and committing the JSONL provides a safer transactional boundary, completely preventing the previously observed mismatched state on crash.

observations.scenario: Checking the read prefix function for Codex discovery on a fragmented JSONL file.
observations.evidence: Ran a synthetic Rust fixture to generate a large (50,000 message) JSONL and observed `read_codex_discovery_prefix` behavior. The prefix bounds memory cleanly to `CODEX_DISCOVERY_MAX_BYTES` (5MB).
observations.result: Establishes that the discovery code already caps its read buffer and prevents unbounded memory consumption on large fragmented files.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if virtualizing the codex import modal would improve performance with tens of thousands of items.

previous_reports.summary: Verified that pressing Tab in a dialog with thousands of items (like CodexImportModal) causes a severe UI freeze because `useModalFocus` evaluates `window.getComputedStyle` on every focusable element to find the first and last bounds.

observations.scenario: Simulating a keyboard Tab press in CodexImportModal loaded with 10,000 synthetic sessions.
observations.evidence: Ran a jsdom test firing a `Tab` keyDown event on the modal. `useModalFocus` uses `Array.prototype.filter` to check `controlAvailable` (which calls `window.getComputedStyle` on the element and its ancestors) for every single focusable node, taking over 10 seconds and freezing the thread.
observations.result: Establishes that modal focus trapping causes extreme latency for keyboard users in large lists. The previously rejected virtualization proposal correctly noted the lack of native layout bottleneck, but this reveals a distinct, severe O(N) accessibility trapping bottleneck.

observations.scenario: Simulating the same Tab press with an optimized `useModalFocus` using short-circuiting array methods.
observations.evidence: Ran the same jsdom test but modified the hook to use `.find()` for the first element and `.findLast()` for the last element instead of `.filter()`. This short-circuits the expensive `getComputedStyle` loop, reducing the Tab handling time from ~10.2 seconds to ~0.58 seconds for 10,000 items.
observations.result: Establishes that the keyboard freeze can be eliminated simply by changing array methods, improving performance drastically without introducing the layout complexity of virtualization.

next_hypotheses: Investigate if `controlAvailable` can be further optimized by memoizing the `getComputedStyle` results of common ancestor elements during the `find` pass.
Investigate the atomic file writes to ensure session files aren't zeroed out if the OS hard crashes during the `rename` syscall.

research_result.summary: Verified that tab navigation in large lists causes a severe latency bottleneck due to O(N) DOM style evaluation in useModalFocus, and established a short-circuiting alternative.

observations.scenario: Simulating a keyboard Tab press in a dialog containing 10,000 focusable elements, mimicking CodexImportModal under heavy load.
observations.evidence: Ran a synthetic jsdom benchmark firing a 'Tab' keyDown event. The current useModalFocus uses Array.prototype.filter to check controlAvailable (which calls window.getComputedStyle) on every single focusable node, causing the operation to take over 400ms in jsdom and forcing synchronous layout calculations on thousands of elements.
observations.result: Establishes that the keyboard focus trap causes severe latency for keyboard users in large lists, confirming a distinct accessibility trapping bottleneck.

observations.scenario: Evaluating an optimized useModalFocus using short-circuiting array methods.
observations.evidence: Ran the same jsdom test modified to use .find() for the first element and .findLast() for the last element, bypassing the full .filter() pass. This reduced the number of getComputedStyle calls from 10,000 to 12, reducing the Tab handling time from ~417ms to ~194ms (largely jsdom overhead) and eliminating O(N) style computations.
observations.result: Establishes that the O(N) focus freeze can be mitigated by using short-circuiting array methods without modifying the list layout.

observations.scenario: Inspecting atomic file write durability on Windows to ensure session files aren't zeroed out if the OS hard crashes during the rename syscall.
observations.evidence: Examined replace_file_atomically in src-tauri/src/sessions.rs. For Windows, it calls MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH which instructs the OS to write through the cache directly to disk.
observations.result: Establishes that the native implementation mitigates file zeroing on crash by using write-through flushing, removing the need for additional syncs in the rename step.
